'''''Sium suave''''', the '''water parsnip''' or '''hemlock waterparsnip''', is a [[Perennial plant|perennial]] wildflower in the family [[Apiaceae]]. It is native to many areas of both Asia and North America. The common name water parsnip is due to its similarity to parsnip (''[[Parsnip|Pastinaca sativa]]'') and its wetland habitat. The alternate common name hemlock waterparsnip is due to its similarity to the highly poisonous spotted water hemlock (''[[Cicuta maculata]]'').

==Introduction==
''Sium suave,'' also widely known as water parsnip, is a wildflower native to parts of the northern hemisphere<ref name=":32">{{Cite web|url=http://www.tropicos.org/Name/1700243?tab=distribution|title=Tropicos {{!}} Name - Sium suave Walter|website=www.tropicos.org|access-date=2016-11-03}}</ref> and thriving in primarily [[wetland]] habitats.<ref name=":15">{{Cite web|url=http://www.illinoiswildflowers.info/wetland/plants/wt_parsnip.html|title=Water Parsnip (Sium suave)|website=www.illinoiswildflowers.info|access-date=2016-11-03}}</ref> ''Sium suave'' belongs to the carrot family, Apiaceae.<ref name=":23">{{Cite web|url=http://herbarium.unc.edu/flora.htm|title=UNC Herbarium|website=herbarium.unc.edu|access-date=2016-10-31|archive-date=2018-10-06|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181006082209/http://herbarium.unc.edu/flora.htm|url-status=dead}}</ref> Water parsnip blooms from July to August<ref name=":04">{{Cite web|url=http://www.pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Sium+suave|title=Sium suave Water Parsnip}}</ref> and creates many small white flowers with umbel inflorescences.<ref name=":42">{{Cite web|url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=200015945|title=Sium suave in Flora of China @ efloras.org|website=www.efloras.org|access-date=2016-11-03}}</ref> ''Sium suave'' resembles a few quite poisonous plants, and consumption should be avoided.<ref name=":04"/> There is a vast number of insect species of bees, beetles, wasps, butterflies, and flies that visit this plant for its nectar and pollen.<ref name=":15"/> ''Sium'' come from the Latin ''sion'' meaning water parsley, and ''suave'' comes from the Latin ''suâvis meaning sweet.''<ref name=":53">{{Cite web|url=http://www.rook.org/earl/bwca/nature/aquatics/sium.html|title=Water Parsnip, Sium suave|last=Rook|first=Earl J.S.|website=www.rook.org|access-date=2016-11-08|archive-date=2007-10-15|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071015002649/http://www.rook.org/earl/bwca/nature/aquatics/sium.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Description==
The shape and size of the leaves depends on the environment in which ''S. suave'' grows. Basal rosette leaves form on moist ground at around 3.8 cm long, and in shallow water they grow in clusters of aquatic leaves.<ref name=":15"/> Once leaves are formed this flowering plant stands up to 3 meters tall with stems that are 5 cm in diameter.<ref name=":23"/> Water parsnip has light green and glabrous stems with longitudinal veins and few branches. Leaves along the stems are alternate and odd-pinnate.<ref name=":15"/> Water parsnip flowers are perfect (both male and female) and are self-fertile.<ref name=":04"/> The pedicels are 3–5 mm long and the fruit is ovoid. The fruit is dry but does not split open when ripe. The flowers have umbellule inflorescence with 10-20 white flowers.<ref name=":42"/> These white flowers are small (~3.2 mm across) with 5 petals. The petals can sometimes be of unequal size and are somewhat heart shaped.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.minnesotawildflowers.info/flower/water-parsnip|title=Sium suave (Water Parsnip): Minnesota Wildflowers|website=www.minnesotawildflowers.info|access-date=2016-11-06}}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
''Sium suave'' is a member of the order [[Apiales]] and the family [[Apiaceae]], the celery, carrot and parsley family (also known as Umbelliferae). This family contains about 445 genera and about 3540 species. Some distinctive characteristics of this family include compound leaf, simple or compound umbel inflorescence containing many small flowers, 2 styles, 2-carpellate ovary, and a schizocarp fruit that splits into 2 mericarps. This species belongs to the genus ''Sium'' which is made up of about 9 species. Species in ''Sium'' are all perennial herbs of the northern hemisphere.<ref name=":23"/> Some common characteristics of this genus include serrate leaves with teeth turned inward and slightly overlapping, flowers in bracteate umbels with conspicuous involucels, five small teeth on calyx, white petals that are obcordate with inflexed apex, styles with depressed conical base which spread or recurve above, fruit that are laterally flattened with mericarp exhibiting 5 ridges, and subterete seeds.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://biodiversityadvisor.sanbi.org/wp-content/themes/bst/keys/e-Key-20160604/Genera/G_Sium.html|title=Apiaceae - Apioideae - Sium L.|work=Keys to Flora of Southern Africa, biodiversityadvisor.sanbi.org/}}</ref> The diploid number of chromosomes for Suim suave is 22.<ref>{{Cite journal|journal=Canadian Journal of Botany |volume=39 | doi=10.1139/b61-092|title=Chromosome Numbers of Canadian Weeds. III |year=1961 |last1=Mulligan |first1=Gerald A. |issue=5 |pages=1057–1066 |bibcode=1961CaJB...39.1057M }}</ref> The [[Kutenai people|Kutenai]] call water parsnip '''''nakhankam''''' ([[Kutenai language|Ktunaxa]]: naq̓an̓kam).<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.firstvoices.ca/en/Ktunaxa/word-category/e599527968bd1f59/--Plants---food-plants|title=FirstVoices- Ktunaxa. Plants: food plants: words.|access-date=2012-07-07|archive-date=2015-09-24|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150924013322/http://www.firstvoices.ca/en/Ktunaxa/word-category/e599527968bd1f59/--Plants---food-plants|url-status=dead}}</ref> ''Sium suave'' (from the [[Latin]] ''sium'', the Latinization of Greek ''sion'', meaning "water parsley," and ''suâvis'', meaning "sweet."), the hemlock waterparsnip or water parsnip, is a [[herb]] native to parts of Canada, Asia, and North America. Synonyms for ''S. suave'' include ''Sium'' ''cicutifolium'' Schrank, ''Sium'' ''floridanum'' Small, ''Sium'' ''suave'' Walter var. ''floridanum'' (Small) C.F. Reed,<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://plants.usda.gov/plant-profile?symbol=SISU2|title=Plants Profile for Sium suave (hemlock waterparsnip)|website=plants.usda.gov|access-date=2016-10-31}}</ref> ''Apium'' ''cicutifolia'' (J.F.Gmel.) Benth. & Hook.f. ex F.B.Forbes & Hemsl., ''Cicuta'' ''dahurica'' Fisch. ex Schultz, ''Sium'' ''cicutifolium'' Schrenk, ''Sium'' ''formosanum'' Hayata, and ''Sium'' ''nipponicum'' Maxim.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.theplantlist.org/tpl1.1/record/kew-2473874|title=Sium suave Walter — The Plant List|website=www.theplantlist.org|access-date=2016-10-31}}</ref> According to a molecular phylogeny created with maximum parsimony heuristic searches using a 59-sequence data set of ''Sium'' s.l., ''Helosciadium'', ''Cryptotaenia'', and outgroups, the sister groups of ''S. suave'' are ''Sium medium'' found in Central Asia and ''Sium latifolium'' found in Western Europe, Eastern Europe, and Western Asia.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Spalik|first=Krzysztof|year=2006|title=The evolutionary history of Sium sensu lato (Apiaceae): dispersal, vicariance, and domestication as inferred from ITS rDNA phylogeny1|journal=American Journal of Botany|volume=93|issue=5|pages=747–761|doi=10.3732/ajb.93.5.747|pmid=21642138 |bibcode=2006AmJB...93..747S }}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
''Sium suave'' grows in wetland habitats (sandy and non-sandy). These wetland habits include wet prairies, bottoms of seeps, low areas along springs, soggy thickets, swamps, borders and shallow water of ponds, marshes, and ditches.<ref name=":15"/> It is native to both North America and Asia in Canada, the United States, Japan, Russian Federation, South Korea, and China.<ref name=":32"/>

==Uses==
Extreme caution should be practiced when using this plant for food because it resembles the very poisonous ''[[Cicuta maculata]]'' (Spotted Water Hemlock).{{efn|The Spotted Water Hemlock possesses a few traits that water parsnip does not: purplish mottling on the stem, multiple leaflet divisions, and leaflet veins ending in notches.<ref name=":53"/>}} Edible parts of ''Sium suave'' include the root in the spring and fall, either raw or cooked; it has a nutty flavor. The leaves are also sometimes used for condiments such as relish. Crushed water parsnip roots have also been used as an analgesic (pain reliever) in cases of broken limbs.<ref name=":04"/>

==Cultivation==
Water parsnip should be grown in wet mucky soil / sand or in standing water up to an inch and a half deep. It also prefers partial to full sun.<ref name=":15"/> The seeds should be sown in late winter to early spring during a cold frame. ''Sium suave'' is in flower from July to August while the seeds ripen from September to October.<ref name=":04"/> It has been shown to accumulate arsenic and heavy metals near abandoned mine tailings in South Korea.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Concentrations of arsenic and heavy metals in vegetation at two abandoned mine tailings in South Korea|journal=Environmental Geochemistry and Health|volume=27|bibcode=2005EnvGH..27..109C |last1=Chang |first1=Peichun |last2=Kim |first2=Ju-Yong |last3=Kim |first3=Kyoung-Woong |date=2005 |issue=2 |page=109 |doi=10.1007/s10653-005-0130-7 |pmid=16003579 }}</ref> In the presence of added N03-N to the ground, water parsnip shows increased production.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Effects of Phalaris arundinacea and Nitrate-N Addition on the Establishment of Wetland Plant Communities|journal= Journal of Applied Ecology|volume=39|bibcode=2002JApEc..39..134G |last1=Green |first1=Emily K. |last2=Galatowitsch |first2=Susan M. |date=2002 |issue=1 |page=134 |doi=10.1046/j.1365-2664.2002.00702.x }}</ref>

==Faunal associations==
These flowers attract a wide variety of insects. While most insects are attracted to the nectar of the flower, bees seek both their nectar and pollen. These include 21 species of bees, 73 species of flies, 91 species of wasps,4 species of plant bugs, 5 species of butterflies, and 19 species of beetles.<ref name=":15"/> Two types of physodermas have been found to parasitize ''S. suave''. Type I physoderm causes conspicuous black pustules on several parts of the plant including the stem, petiole, leaflet lemina, and flowers. Type II physoderma formed abundant resting spores and epibiotic sporangia on seedlings of ''S. suave''.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=OBSERVATIONS ON CHYTRIDIACEOUS PARASITES OF PHANEROGAMS. XXVIII. PHYSODERMAS ON SIUM SUAVE|journal=Mycological Society of America|volume=71}}</ref> The stems and leaves of this plant are toxic to livestock.<ref name=":53"/>
